name: The Seebeck Effect
statement: A temperature difference across a material generates a voltage, turning heat straight into electricity.
meaning: The Seebeck effect is the appearance of a voltage across an electrical conductor, or between two dissimilar conductors, when a temperature difference is imposed along it. A hot end and a cold end give rise to an electromotive force, a direct conversion of a temperature gradient into a thermoelectric voltage. The ratio of the induced voltage to the temperature difference is the material's Seebeck coefficient, or thermopower. Discovered by Thomas Johann Seebeck in 1821, the effect is the basis of the thermocouple, the most common electronic temperature sensor, and of thermoelectric generators that turn heat directly into electricity. Together with its reverse, the Peltier effect, and the Thomson effect, it makes up the thermoelectric effects that link heat flow and electric current in materials.
mechanism: The effect arises because charge carriers at the hot end have more thermal energy and diffuse toward the cold end faster than carriers diffuse back, building up a charge imbalance and hence a voltage that opposes further diffusion. How strongly this happens depends on the material, captured by its Seebeck coefficient, and the sign of the coefficient depends on whether the carriers are negative electrons or positive holes. Joining two different materials, whose coefficients differ, into a loop with the junctions at different temperatures produces a net measurable voltage, the working principle of the thermocouple. The reverse effect, in which a current forced through a junction pumps heat and creates a temperature difference, is the Peltier effect, the basis of solid-state cooling.

examples.text: Two dissimilar metals joined at a hot and a cold junction produce a voltage that measures temperature, the ubiquitous thermocouple sensor used across science and industry.
Thermoelectric generators convert the heat of decaying radioisotopes directly into electricity by the Seebeck effect, powering deep-space probes like the Voyager craft.
Running a current through a junction the other way pumps heat, the Peltier effect Jean Peltier found in 1834, used in compact solid-state coolers.

variants.name: The Peltier effect
variants.text: The reverse thermoelectric effect, in which an electric current through a junction of two materials produces heating or cooling, used for solid-state refrigeration.

variants.name: The Thomson effect
variants.text: The heating or cooling of a single current-carrying conductor that also has a temperature gradient along it, predicted by William Thomson in 1851.

whyItMatters: The Seebeck effect is the foundation of temperature measurement by thermocouples, which are among the most widely used sensors in science and engineering, and of solid-state conversion of heat into electricity. Thermoelectric generators built on it power spacecraft far from the Sun, harvest waste heat, and supply remote sensors with no moving parts. Together with the Peltier effect it enables compact refrigeration and precise thermal control.

working.text: impose a temperature difference across a conductor and read the thermoelectric voltage it produces, proportional to the difference through the Seebeck coefficient.
join two dissimilar conductors with junctions at different temperatures so their differing coefficients give a net voltage that measures temperature.
drive a current through a junction to move heat by the Peltier effect, the basis of solid-state coolers, the inverse of the Seebeck effect.

limits: The Seebeck effect depends on the temperature difference and the material pair, not on absolute temperature, so a uniform-temperature conductor produces no voltage. It and the Peltier effect are reverse phenomena, distinct though related, and conflating them muddles which converts heat to voltage and which uses current to move heat. The voltages produced are typically small, microvolts per degree, so thermocouples need careful calibration and reference junctions, and thermoelectric generators convert heat to electricity at modest efficiency, limited by the properties of available materials, which is why the search for better thermoelectrics continues.
misreadings: The effect responds to a temperature difference across the material and the material pairing, not to how hot it is in absolute terms, so equal temperatures give no voltage however high. The Seebeck effect, temperature difference to voltage, and the Peltier effect, current to temperature difference, are opposites, not the same phenomenon. And while Seebeck first observed it in 1821 as a deflected compass needle, calling it thermomagnetism, the effect is electrical, the magnetism merely a symptom of the current his thermoelectric voltage drove.
origin: Discovered by Thomas Johann Seebeck in 1821, who observed a compass needle deflected by a circuit of two metals held at different temperatures; its reverse, the Peltier effect, was found by Jean Peltier in 1834, and the Thomson effect predicted by William Thomson in 1851.
